question: The Cyprus Council for the Recognition of Higher Education Qualifications does not recognise a higher education qualification awarded by Staffordshire University, a university recognised by other Member States and an institution recognised by the European Higher Education Area (EHEA).
The refusal is based on the fact that the programme of study is delivered, in whole or in part, through a partner institution in Cyprus.

However, according to the case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, notably in Cases C-153/02 (Neri v European School of Economics)1 and C-274/05 (Commission v Hellenic Republic)2, the decisive factor for recognition should be the awarding institution rather than the place, or mode of delivery, of the studies. In this context: 1.
Does the Commission consider that such a refusal is compatible with Articles 49 and 56 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union?
Has the Commission identified similar practices in other Member States concerning qualifications delivered through franchised or validated arrangements?
Can the Commission take action, including infringement procedures, to ensure compliance with EU law and the principles of mutual recognition within the EHEA?

Judgment of the Court of Justice of 13 November 2003, Valentina Neri v European School of Economics (ESE Insight World Education System Ltd), Case C-153/02, ECLI:EU:C:2003:614. Judgment of the Court of Justice of 23 October 2008, Commission of the European Communities v Hellenic Republic, Case C-274/05, ECLI:EU:C:2008:585.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.6.2026) The European Higher Education Area (EHEA) was created under the intergovernmental Bologna Process, which comprises 47 countries cooperating on a voluntary basis. Therefore, it is not regulated by EU law and falls within the exclusive sphere of competence of the signatory countries.
Whilst recognition based on robust quality assurance is the core of the EHEA, it is an obligation of Member States to oversee its implementation.

Moreover, Article 165(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) provides that the EU shall contribute to the development of quality education by encouraging cooperation between Member States while fully respecting ‘the responsibility of the Member States for the content of teaching and the organisation of education systems’, including recognition of degrees for the purpose of further learning (academic recognition of qualifications).

It also applies to cases where qualifications are delivered through franchised or validated arrangements. Finally, based on the available information, Staffordshire University is a university in the United Kingdom – a third country in relation to the EU. The initial recognition of a degree from a third country falls under the competence of the Member State in which the recognition application is submitted.
The Commission has no authority to intervene in case of refusal by the Member State to recognise third country qualifications. Articles 49 and 56 TFEU do not apply in the present case.
